title: Stop before it spills
hook: better to stop than to fill a cup to the brim; retire when the work is done (Tao Te Ching 9)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter eight, and your line was like water: go around, and keep going. Did something block your way? Water fills things. Chapter nine asks how full is too full. Day one thousand seventy-one.

A mug of coffee, poured right to the rim, being carried from the counter to the couch. Every step is a negotiation. Eyes locked on the surface. Tiny shuffling steps. A little slops over anyway, onto the hand, onto the rug, and the whole walk is spent guarding the cup instead of enjoying it. One more splash from the pot made all of that happen. Leave a finger's width at the top and the walk is easy. Chapter nine of the Tao Te Ching opens with a full vessel of its own, and then gives three more pictures like it.
screen: `POURED RIGHT TO THE RIM.` → `GUARDING THE CUP.` → `ONE MORE SPLASH.`

segments.voice: First, the cup. Legge's translation begins: "It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full." Not empty. Just not full to the brim. The last bit of filling is what makes the carrying hard. Second, the blade. Keep sharpening an edge, the chapter says, and it won't keep its sharpness for long. Past a point, more work on the blade only wears it away. Third, the hall of treasure. Fill a hall with gold and jade, it goes on, and no one can guard it all. And when wealth and honor make someone proud, they bring harm on themselves. Four pictures: a cup, a blade, a treasure hall, a proud name. Each one is something good, pushed one step too far. The chapter isn't against coffee, or sharp knives, or wealth. It's about the extra splash. Fourth, the way of heaven. Then the chapter's last line, in Legge's words: "When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven." Seasons do this. Summer doesn't stay on to be admired. It does its work, steps back, and autumn comes. Stopping, in this chapter, isn't failure or quitting. It's knowing when the work is done.
screen: `THE CUP: NOT TO THE BRIM.` · `THE BLADE: SHARPENED AWAY.` · `THE HALL: TOO MUCH TO GUARD.` · `THE WORK DONE, STEP BACK.` · then, large: `STOP BEFORE IT SPILLS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to stop one thing before it's too much, and the sit is where you find it. Settle, and breathe. Look at today and tomorrow. Where are you about to pour one more splash? One more email tonight, one more episode, one more edit to something already finished, one more thing added to a full week. Pick the one. Picture yourself stopping a little short of the rim, and notice what it's like to carry the cup with room at the top. If you pray, you can ask for help stopping. If you don't, just breathe with the room you've left. The bell holds the time.
Stop before it spills. Chapter nine's cup, blade, treasure hall and proud name, and its last line: when the work is done, step back. Today's word.

Your line: stop before it spills. Today, stop that one thing short of the rim. A week of chapters ends here: no contest, untie the knot, not personal, the valley, last and first, like water, and now this. Day one thousand seventy-one.

howItsDone: Some readers use chapter nine as a check on overwork and excess, choosing to stop a task when it is done well enough rather than polishing or adding past that point.

original.note: Chinese, gōng suì shēn tuì: the work done, the self withdraws. From the close of Tao Te Ching 9.

trapdoor: what you thought: stop before it spills means don't try too hard.
what it means: a cup, a blade, a treasure hall and a proud name, each good thing pushed one step too far; when the work is done, step back.
what a scholar hears: the chapter calls stepping back after the work is done the way of heaven, like seasons that finish and give way.
